f: What are the literal and technical definitions of taqlid?
b:
• Literal definition: The verbal noun derived from the Arabic root q-l-d, which means to place, gird, or adorn with a necklace. 

• Technical definition: The acceptance of another's statement without demanding proof or evidence, on the belief that the statement is being made in accordance with fact and proof.

f: How is taqlid present and necessary in everyday life, language, learning, and society?
b:
• Language & Learning: If we had refused to accept unquestionably (without demanding proof) the commands and teachings of our parents and teachers, we would not have learned our mother tongue, the alphabet, or the study and writing of books. 

• Specialized Knowledge: Proficiency in any branch of knowledge requires accepting its technical terminology and linguistic usages through taqlid (without questioning the authority of the terminology). 

• Social & Practical Life: Human life—eating, drinking, walking, earning—and societal progress (such as an army following a commander's orders or governments enforcing laws) are firmly rooted in taqlid (accepting and obeying professional authority).

f: What are the two types of wujub (compulsory nature) in jurisprudence (wujub bi 'l-dhat and wujub bi 'l-ghayr), and how do they apply to the preservation of the Qur'an and Hadith versus taqlid?
b:
• Wujub bi 'l-dhat ("compulsory in itself"): Acts ordered or prohibited by Islamic law due to their intrinsic nature, like the command of prayer and the prohibition of polytheism. 

• Wujub bi 'l-ghayr ("compulsory due to an external factor"): Acts that are not compulsory in themselves, but constitute the basis for other actions that are specifically commanded or prohibited in the Qur'an and hadiths. 

• Application: Preserving the Qur'an and hadith is categorically commanded (wujub bi 'l-dhat). Because such preservation is not normally possible without recording them in writing, writing them down has been decreed as wajib (wujub bi 'l-ghayr) based on necessity and the consensus of the Umma. In the exact same way, taqlid ("following someone in matters of Islamic law") is also decreed as essential or wajib.

f: How does the hadith of Aswad ibn Yazid (Sahih al-Bukhari 2:297) regarding Mu'adh ibn Jabal رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ in Yemen serve as evidence for the validity and practice of taqlid and taqlid shakhsi during the time of the Prophet ﷺ?
b:
• Example of Taqlid: When Mu'adh رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ decreed half the estate for a daughter and half for a sister, the questioner accepted the ruling without demanding proof or a basis, relying on Mu'adh's رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ integrity, piety, and righteousness. 

• Approval by the Messenger ﷺ: The Prophet ﷺ did not criticize the people for following Mu'adh رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, nor did he raise any objections. 

• Proof for Taqlid Shakhsi: The Prophet ﷺ appointed Mu'adh رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ to provide religious instruction to the people of Yemen, granting them the right and permission to refer to Mu'adh رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ in all affairs of the Din, demonstrating that following a particular person in Islamic law was prevalent during the time of the Messenger ﷺ.

f: What are some of the stated negative consequences and evils of discarding taqlid?
b:
• People do not model their lives after the example of the Prophet ﷺ, leading to selfishness, corrupt motives, lust, anarchy, and opposition to consensus. 

• The absence of taqlid shakhsi leads to the rise of self-appointed mujtahids who consider themselves capable of inferring rulings through analogical reasoning (qiyas), claiming equal or greater rank than early mujtahids. 

• It opens the door to modernist claims—such as arguing that wudu' for prayer was merely for early Arabs exposed to impurities and is no longer necessary under modern hygiene—undermining clear rulings of the Shari'a.

f: How does Mufti Taqi 'Uthmani respond to the objection that following an Imam in matters of Shari'a is shirk (polytheism) or a reprehensible innovation (bid'a)?
b:
• True Obedience: True obedience belongs to Allah alone. Obedience to the Messenger ﷺ is ordered because he conveyed divine commands, and consulting a scholar (alim) or jurist (imam) to know how to obey Allah does not mean taking them as the subject of obedience. 

• Necessity of Expertise: Deriving rules from the Qur'an and Sunna requires intensive study and mastery of Arabic and related sciences, which is impossible for every individual. Allah ordained in Qur'an 9:122 that a group should devote themselves to acquiring knowledge so others can consult them. 

• Essence of Taqlid: Taqlid is simply a person who cannot independently interpret the sources consulting a qualified jurist and acting upon their interpretation to fulfill the requirements of the Shari'a without committing shirk.

f: What is a madhhab ("school"), and how does following a particular school relate to following the Qur'an and Sunna?
b:
• Definition of Madhhab: A madhhab is a particular interpretation of the Shari'a and a collection of major shari' rules derived from the Holy Qur'an and Sunna by a reliable jurist, arranged subject-wise for the convenience of followers. 

• Relationship to Sources: The school of an Imam is not parallel or alien to the Shari'a; rather, someone who follows a particular school is actually following the Qur'an and Sunna according to the interpretation of a reliable, trustworthy jurist whom they believe is well-versed in matters of Shari'a.

f: What are the two types of rules mentioned in the Holy Qur'an and Sunna regarding interpretation, and what are the three main causes for differences of opinion among the various schools?
b:
• Two Types of Rules:

1. Clear rules allowing only one interpretation: Rules stated so clearly (such as prayer, zakat, fasting, pilgrimage, prohibition of pork and adultery) that all schools are unanimous, leaving no room for ijtihad, taqlid, or consulting an Imam. 

2. Rules allowing multiple interpretations: Rules derived where different situations or interpretations arise. 

• Three Causes for Differences of Opinion:

1. Wording with multiple interpretations: E.g., the word quru' in Qur'an 2:228 meaning either "menstruation" (Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ) or "cleanliness/tuhr" (Shafi'i). 

2. Disparity between two hadiths: E.g., differing traditions regarding raising hands while bowing (ruku') in prayer. 

3. Unaddressed issues: Issues not specifically addressed in the Qur'an and Sunna, requiring solution through analogy (qiyas) or examples.

f: How do the schools of the four Imams compare to other schools, which school should a person follow, and how does the legal analogy of lower courts following a high court apply to madhhabs?
b:
• The Four Schools: While many jurists practiced ijtihad, the schools of the four Imams (Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, Malik, Shafi'i, Ahmad) became the most comprehensive, well-arranged, and well-preserved, and the Umma has taken them as having the most reliable interpretations. 

• Which School to Follow: All recognized schools are sincere and equally valid; a person should follow the school of any recognized Imam whom they believe to be most knowledgeable and pious. 

• Legal Analogy: Just as lower courts and citizens follow high court judgements (treating the high court as a trustworthy interpreter of the law, not a legislator), a Muslim following a jurist's school is following a trustworthy interpreter of the Shari'a, without accusing anyone of disregarding the law or committing shirk.

f: Why is "pick-and-mix" (talfiq) between different schools condemned for a non-professional layman, and how does it lead to following personal desires?
b:
• Following Desires over Evidence: A layman lacking the ability to compare arguments, if left free to choose any view, will naturally select views that fulfill personal convenience or desires rather than the strength of evidence—a practice condemned by the Qur'an. 

• Contradictory Combination Example: For instance, choosing the Hanafi view on touching a woman (doesn't break wudu') and the Shafi'i view on bleeding (doesn't break wudu') leaves a person acting upon a composite state that would be considered invalid by both schools combined. 

• Preventing Anarchy: The policy of allegiance to a single school (taqlid shakhsi) was adopted by jurists as a preventive measure to preclude anarchy in the Shari'a and stop people from treating the law as a plaything.

f: What are the exceptions where a person or qualified scholar may adopt a view from another madhhab?
b:
• Those Qualified in Ijtihad: Individuals equipped with the necessary qualifications of ijtihad do not need to follow a particular school and can derive rules directly from original sources. 

• Qualified Scholars / Experts: Those well-versed in Islamic disciplines who can evaluate different juristic views purely on academic grounds (without personal desires) are not forbidden from preferring one school over another in a specific matter. 

• Juristic Preference (Tarjih): Sometimes Hanafi jurists, after comprehensive study, conclude that another Imam's view is stronger based on evidence.

f: Why might jurists sometimes depart from the view of their own Imam, and what is required to adopt another school's view?
b:
• Grounds for Departure: Jurists may depart from their Imam's view if an analogy does not conform to an authentic hadith (which the Imam likely did not know of), or out of necessity for the collective good of the Umma in changing circumstances. 

• Conditions for Adopting Another View: Because all four schools rest on solid grounds, a competent scholar with the required knowledge, academic research capabilities, and freedom from personal desires may adopt another school's view. Those lacking these conditions must not do so to prevent legal anarchy.

f: Why does superficial self-study of translated texts lead to unjustified criticism of former jurists, and what does true extraction of juridical rules require?
b:
• Superficial Study Dangers: Individuals relying on cursory translation study often assume mastery and unjustifiably criticize former jurists out of ignorance. 

• Requirements for Rule Extraction: Extracting rules requires collecting scattered material across chapters, examining hadith veracity via usul al-hadith, studying historical backgrounds, and resolving complex issues—a level of intensive knowledge rarely found in contemporary non-specialists.

f: What is the definition of a tabi'i (Follower) according to the majority of hadith scholars, and how does Imam Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ hold a unique status among the four Imams in this regard?
b:
• Definition: According to the majority of hadith scholars (preferred by Hafiz Ibn Hajar al-'Asqalani, Allama Iraqi, Ibn al-Salah, Nawawi, and Hakim), a tabi'i is someone who met a Companion (Sahabi) of the Messenger ﷺ or merely saw one while in a state of faith (iman). It is not necessary for him to have remained in their company or to have narrated from them. 

• Unique Status: Imam Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ (born 80 A.H.) is confirmed by biographers and historians to be a tabi'i, having seen the Companion Anas ibn Malik رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ multiple times when Anas رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ visited Kufa. This is a unique rank held by him that cannot be said regarding the other three great Imams (Malik, Shafi'i, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal).

f: Which Companions (Sahaba) did Imam Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ meet or narrate from, as recorded by scholars like Ibn Hajar al-Makki, Khatib al-Baghdadi, Daraqutni, and Imam 'Abd al-Qadir al-Misri?
b:
• Seeing Anas ibn Malik رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ: Ibn Hajar al-Makki (al-Khayrat al-hisan), Khatib al-Baghdadi (Tarikh al-Baghdad), and Daraqutni (Tabyid al-sahifa) all confirm that Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ saw Anas ibn Malik رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ. 

• Companions Narrated From: According to Imam 'Abd al-Qadir al-Misri (al-Fawa'id al-bahiyya 42), the Companions from whom Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ related hadiths include: 'Abdullah ibn Unays, 'Abdullah ibn Jaz'a al-Zabidi, Anas ibn Malik رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, Jabir ibn 'Abdullah رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, Ma'qil ibn Yasar, Wathila ibn al-Asqa', and 'A'isha رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا bint 'l-Ajrad ؓ.

f: What account does Imam Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ give regarding his meeting with the Companion 'Abdullah ibn al-Harith ibn Jaz'a ؓ during Hajj in 93 A.H.?
b:
• Imam Abu Yusuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ relates that Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ said he performed Hajj with his father in 93 A.H. when he was 16 years old. 

• He saw a crowd gathered around a teacher who his father identified as the Companion 'Abdullah ibn al-Harith ibn Jaz'a ؓ. 

• Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ got close enough to hear him report that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever acquires an understanding of the religion of Allah, Allah suffices him in his matters of concern and provides him with sustenance from sources which he could not expect."

f: How do statements from scholars such as Hafiz al-Sam'ani, Makki ibn Ibrahim, 'Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak, and Imam Shafi'i describe Imam Abu Hanifa's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ mastery of knowledge and status as a jurist?
b:
• Hafiz al-Sam'ani: Recounts that when visiting Abbasid caliph Mansur, 'Isa ibn Musa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ pointed to Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and declared, "This is the scholar of the world today" (al-Ansab 247). 

• Makki ibn Ibrahim (Shaykh of Imam Bukhari): Remembered him as the greatest scholar of his time (I'la' al-sunan 18:308). 

• 'Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak: Stated that when he inquired in Kufa about the most learned, devout, and knowledgeable person, scholars unanimously answered that it was Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, noting they knew of no one else possessing such characteristics (al-Mizan 58). He also remarked, "The greatest jurist is Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ. I have not seen anyone like him in the field of jurisprudence". 

• Imam Shafi'i: Remarked that people are dependent on Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ in the field of jurisprudence (Tahdhib al-Tahdhib 10:450), and when asked if Imam Malik met Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, Malik replied that he had seen a person who, if he said he could turn a pillar into gold, would be able to provide evidence for it (Tabyid al-sahifa 16).

f: How do scholars ('Allama Zafar 'Uthmani and Muhammad ibn Sama'a) explain Imam Abu Hanifa's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ extensive transmission and mastery of hadith?
b:
• Muhammad ibn Sama'a: States that the Imam mentioned more than 70,000 hadiths in his books and selected the Athar from 40,000 hadiths. 

• 'Allama Zafar 'Uthmani: Explains that all of the Imam's legal rulings (masa'il) are in actual fact hadiths narrated in the form of legal rulings rather than formal narrations. Furthermore, he compiled formal narrations through his personal chains that were collected in his students' Masanid and works (such as Imam Muhammad's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ Kitab al-athar, Muwatta, Hujaj; Abu Yusuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Ibn al-Mubarak's works; Waki's Musnad; and collections by Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd al-Razzaq, Hakim, Ibn Hibban, Bayhaqi, and others). 

• Status as a Hadith Critic: Imam Dhahabi includes Imam Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ in his Tadhkirat al-huffaz among those who possessed prophetic knowledge and could be consulted for their expertise in determining the authenticity or weakness of narrators.

f: How do statements from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, Imam Abu Yusuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, Mulla 'Ali al-Qari رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ (describing the exchange with A'mash), and Ibn al-Mahdi highlight Imam Abu Hanifa's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ profound insight into hadith and evaluation of narrators?
b:
• Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna: Stated that the first person to encourage him to relate hadiths and make him a hadith scholar was Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ. 

• Imam Abu Yusuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ: Stated he never found anyone with more insight into the interpretation of hadiths than Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ. 

• Mulla 'Ali al-Qari رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ (Exchange with A'mash): When Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ recited numerous extended chains of hadiths to A'mash from memory on the spot, A'mash exclaimed, "What took me a hundred days to narrate you repeated to me in just an instance... O group of jurists, you are the physicians, and we are merely the pharmacists". 

• Ibn al-Mahdi: Stated he never saw anyone possessing greater knowledge of the Sunna than Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, noting they only became aware of 'Amr ibn Dinar's agnomen (kunya) through him.

f: What is Ibn Khaldun's conclusive evaluation (Muqaddima) regarding the absurd claim that great jurists like Imam Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ possessed only superficial knowledge of hadith?
b:
• Ibn Khaldun states that it is impossible for someone whom a vast majority of the Umma accepted as a competent jurist to possess only superficial knowledge of hadiths, because Islamic law can only be derived from the Qur'an and Sunna, requiring deep knowledge from the correct source. 

• The trust placed in Abu Hanifa's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ school throughout Islamic history establishes his greatness in the field of hadith.

f: How do Waki' ibn al-Jarrah and Asad ibn al-Furat describe the caliber of Imam Abu Hanifa's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ companions, students, and compilation of works?
b:
• Waki' ibn al-Jarrah (via Tarikh al-Baghdad): Defended Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ by noting how absurd it is to claim he erred when he was surrounded by elite companions and sitting partners of immense caliber in analogy, inference, memorization, and Arabic language (such as Abu Yusuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, Zufar, Muhammad, Yahya ibn Zakariyya, Ibn Abi Za'ida, etc.) who would guide him to the truth. 

• Asad ibn al-Furat (via Imam Tahawi رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ): Noted that the companions of Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ who compiled and recorded his works numbered forty, with those in the forefront being Abu Yusuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, Zufar, Dawud al-Ta'i رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, Asad ibn 'Amr, Yusuf ibn Khalid al-Samti, and Yahya ibn Zakariyya ibn Abi Za'ida (who was his scribe for thirty years).

f: Why is Sayyidina 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud ؓ sometimes targeted with criticism, and what is his true standing among the Companions according to Ahl al-Sunna?
b:
• Reason for Attacks: Because many of his narrations form the basis of numerous opinions in the Hanafi school, some attempt to discredit the Hanafi school by attacking and criticizing this great Companion. 

• Standing and Status: The Companions are considered the most superior and exalted people after the Messengers, and no one after them can attain their status. 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud ؓ is one of the most revered Companions known for his deep understanding of the Qur'an and jurisprudence (fiqh).

f: What grave warnings did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ issue regarding criticizing or troubling his Companions?
b:
• Troubling Companions: The Prophet ﷺ stated that whoever loves them loves them out of love for him, and whoever hates them hates them out of hate for him. Whoever troubles them troubles Allah, and whoever troubles Allah, it is imminent that Allah will seize him (Mishkat al-Masabih, Tirmidhi 554). 

• Cursing Critics: The Prophet ﷺ instructed: "If you come across those who curse my Companions, say, 'May Allah's curse be upon you for your evil'" (Mishkat al-Masabih, Tirmidhi 554). 

• The Stars Metaphor: The Prophet ﷺ described his Companions as like the stars in the skies: "Some are stronger than others but each possesses a light. Whoever adopts any opinion from among the various opinions they differ in will be considered guided in My sight" (Mishkat al-Masabih, Razin al-'Abdari 554).

f: How did Hudhayfa رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ describe 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud's ؓ resemblance to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and what is signified by his agnomen "Ibn Ummi 'Abd"?
b:
• Resemblance: When asked who closely resembled the Messenger ﷺ in manner, conduct, and behavior, Hudhayfa رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ replied: "We are not aware of anyone who possesses a closer resemblance to the Messenger ﷺ in manner, conduct, and habit than Ibn Ummi 'Abd" (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sunan al-Tirmidhi). 

• Agnomen Meaning: "Ummi 'Abd" was his mother's name, meaning that while Hudhayfa رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ was not aware of his private life at home, his public social conduct perfectly mirrored that of the Messenger ﷺ.

f: How did Abu 'l-Darda' describe the status of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud ؓ to 'Alqama when they met in Syria?
b:
• Abu 'l-Darda' remarked: "Do you not have Ibn Ummi 'Abd among you, the keeper of the slippers and pillow of the Messenger ﷺ and the one in charge of his ablution water?" 

• He added that among them was also the one whom Allah protected from Satan, and the keeper of the Prophet's ﷺ secrets which no one else knew.

f: What did 'Umar ibn al-Khattab رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ state regarding 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud's ؓ profound knowledge and trustworthiness?
b:
• 'Umar ibn al-Khattab رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ: Stated that whoever wants to recite the Qur'an as though it were freshly revealed should recite it according to Ibn Mas'ud's رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ recitation. He also described him as "a small person brimming with [the knowledge of] jurisprudence". 

• 'Ali ibn Abi Talib رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ: Stated, "If I were to appoint someone as a leader without consulting [anyone], I would appoint Ibn Ummi 'Abd". Furthermore, the Prophet ﷺ stated: "I am pleased for my Umma with whatever Ibn Ummi 'Abd is pleased with".

f: How do recommendations from the Prophet ﷺ, Mu'adh ibn Jabal رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, and Hudhayfa رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ establish 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud ؓ as a premier source of knowledge?
b:
• The Prophet's ﷺ Directives: Instructed the Umma: "Learn [the knowledge] from four people: 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Salim the slave of Abu Hudhayfa, Ubay ibn Ka'b, and Mu'adh ibn Jabal رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ" (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sunan al-Tirmidhi). The Prophet ﷺ also commanded: "Whatever 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud narrates to you, accept it" (Sunan al-Tirmidhi). 

• Mu'adh ibn Jabal's رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ Deathbed Advice: Advised people to take knowledge from four people, specifically including 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (Sunan al-Tirmidhi). 

• Hudhayfa's رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ Statement: Stated that whatever Hudhayfa رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ relates, accept it, but "however 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud teaches you to recite, recite in that way" (Sunan al-Tirmidhi).

f: How does 'Allama Dhahabi (Tadhkirat al-huffaz) describe the status, character, and caution in narration of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud ؓ?
b:
• Status and Titles: Described as the learned leader (al-imam al-rabbani), Abu 'Abd al-Rahman 'Abdullah ibn Ummi 'Abd al-Hudhali, personal servant and Companion of the Messenger ﷺ.

• Excellence: Among the first to embrace Islam, veterans of Badr, expert jurists, teachers of the Qur'an, and those who strove to convey the Prophet's ﷺ words accurately.

• Caution in Narration: Extremely scrupulous in his narrations, admonishing students who were negligent in recording exact words, and due to extreme caution, narrating very little himself, leading his students to never give preference to any Companion over him.

f: What is the spiritual consequence of criticizing or harboring enmity toward the Companions according to hadith and Qur'anic evidence?
b:
• Declaration of War (Divine Hadith): In a qudsi hadith (Sahih al-Bukhari), the Prophet ﷺ relates that Allah says: "Whoever harbors enmity towards a Friend (wali) of Mine, I declare war against him".

• Serious Crime: Belittling the position of any Companion—especially one endowed with so many virtues—is considered a very serious crime that incurs the wrath of Allah.

• Qur'anic Validation: Allah expresses His eternal pleasure with the Companions in Qur'an 9:100: "Allah is well pleased with them and they pleased with Him. He has prepared for them Gardens under which rivers flow...".

f: What are the common questions regarding foot distance in salat (prayer), and how do scholars generally address this issue?
b:
Common questions include: "How should I stand in prayer [salat]? Should I stand with my legs wide apart so that my feet touch those of the next person? Should I stand at my own comfort and not touch the feet of the next person? or Should I stand with a gap of four fingers between them as some people do?"

Discussions on this point by Islamic scholars are very few compared to other key prayer issues, making the precise views of even the four Imams quite difficult to determine.

f: What is the status of maintaining orderly rows in prayer, and what hadith emphasizes this warning?
b:
Having rows in perfect order is an important sunna (though not a fard/integral), and the imam is responsible for ensuring it before initiating prayer. Narrations carry warnings against disorderly rows, such as: 

"Straighten your rows, or else Allah will create discord between your hearts (Sunan Abi Dawud 1:97)".

f: How does the text analyze the hadith where Companions touched feet together in rows?
b: Upholders of spreading feet wide present a hadith where Companions touched feet together after being commanded to straighten rows. However, the text explains that this hadith does not in any way make joining the feet a wajib (necessary) act.

f: What are the two dominant opinions within the Hanafi school regarding foot positioning during prayer?
b:
1. Four-finger gap: Leaving a gap equal to four fingers of the hand. Radd al-muhtar (1:299) states: "The gap to be left between a person's feet should be equal to that of four fingers of the hand, because this [amount] is very effective in creating [the posture of] submission and humility [sought in prayer]". Jurists consider this superior because standing wide apart causes discomfort and loss of focus. 

2. Personal comfort / No stipulated distance: As noted in Ma'arif al-sunan (2:298), there is no mention in authentic hadith narrations of a stipulated space, so the sunna method is whatever distance a person finds convenient and comfortable while praying.

f: What is reported in Sunan al-Nasa'i regarding 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and the meaning of murawaha?
b:
A hadith in Sunan al-Nasa'i (1:142) states: 

"'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud saw a person standing in prayer with his two feet together [i.e. touching each other] and judged it to be against the sunna. He advised the person that if he had practised murawaha it would have been more preferable". 

While murawaha can mean alternating weight between feet when tired, in this context it most probably means leaving a slight gap between the feet (instructing the person not to join them completely nor spread them too far apart).

f: What are the three recognized opinions of the Shafi'i school regarding the distance between the feet in prayer?
b:
1. A gap equivalent to one hand span between the feet (the most popular view, found in Nihayat al-muhtaj 1:347 U). 

2. A gap equal to four fingers (recommended in al-Anwar, common to both Shafi'i and Hanafi schools). 

3. As much of a gap as the person deems necessary (common to both Shafi'i and Hanafi schools). 

(Note: Imam Nawawi concludes in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab 3:266 U: "It is undesirable [makruh] to join the feet together; it is preferable [mustahab] to keep some distance between them.")

f: What is the full text of the hadith in Sunan Abi Dawud reported by Abu 'l-Qasim al-Jadali regarding joining feet and shoulders?
b: "I heard Nu'man ibn Bashir relate that the Messenger ﷺ faced the people and instructed, 'Straighten your rows. By Allah, you should straighten your rows or else Allah will create disagreement between your hearts.' Nu'man ibn Bashir ﷺ then said, 'I saw each person join his shoulders with those of the next person and his knees and ankles with those of the next person' (Sunan Abi Dawud 1:104)."

f: What key points show that the hadith of Nu'man ibn Bashir does not establish joining feet in salat as necessary (wajib)?
b:
1. The words describing the joining of feet are the narrator's observation of the Companions' reaction to the warning, not a direct command (marfu') from the Messenger ﷺ himself. The Messenger ﷺ merely commanded that lines be straightened. 

2. The narration describes the behavior of the Companions before the prayer began (prior to commencement to align the row) and does not indicate this posture was maintained throughout the prayer. 

3. Not a single juristic opinion in the major schools states that feet must be joined with those of the adjacent person.

f: What logical contradictions and practical difficulties arise if one assumes the joining of feet was maintained throughout the prayer?
b:
1. If required in all postures, joining feet/shoulders in prostration (sujud) or sitting (jalsa/tashahhud) would be practically impossible. 

2. If claimed only for standing (qiyam), maintaining this continuous contact throughout a row during standing is also extremely difficult. 

3. Knees were also mentioned as touching in the hadith of Sunan Abi Dawud; treating this as obligatory would be painful or impossible due to height and size differences between worshippers.

f: How did classical scholars like Hafiz Ibn Hajar and Imam Shawkani interpret the narration/chapter header regarding joining shoulders and feet?
b:
• Hafiz Ibn Hajar (Fath al-Bari 2:247): Explained that Imam Bukhari's chapter title ("Chapter on the Joining of the Shoulders and Feet Together While Forming the Rows") was used to exaggerate (mubalagha) the importance of straightening rows and filling gaps. 

• Imam Shawkani (Nayl al-awtar 3:65 U): Stated the phrase means placing body parts in line so each shoulder is in level with the next person's shoulder, forming a straight line, not that actual physical joining was an obligatory act.

f: What statement did Anas رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ make in Ma'mar's narration (Fath al-Bari 2:247) regarding joining shoulders and feet?
b:
"if I were to attempt this [joining the shoulders and feet together] with anybody today, they would scurry away like restive mules" (Fath al-Bari 2:247). 

Significance: Shows the Companions did not continue this physical practice as a permanent continuous sunna (sunna mustamirra) after the Prophet's ﷺ death.

f: Why is strict foot-joining unnecessary in modern masjids, according to point (7)?
b: Lines are clearly marked on carpets, marble, and floor coverings. Standing with heels aligned on the markings automatically forms perfectly straight rows without needing to force foot-to-foot contact.

f: Why is over-widening the feet (beyond shoulder width) during individual prayer ungrounded according to the text?
b:
1. If everyone in a row stood shoulder-to-shoulder, the gap between one's own feet could naturally only be as wide as the shoulders; spreading wider would make shoulder contact impossible. 

2. Hadiths describing Companions joining feet refer only to congregational alignment and cannot serve as evidence for widening feet during individual salat.

f: What is the author's final summary of the true sunna posture for foot placement in prayer?
b: The true sunna method is to leave a space of approximately four fingers between one's feet, or any gap that allows a comfortable and humble posture. In congregation, worshippers should stand close enough to touch shoulders while keeping heels on the row lines.

f: What differing positions of the hands do people observe when entering various masjids?
b: Some people stand in prayer with their hands clasped together beneath the navel, some folded on the chest, some just beneath the chest, and a few with their hands at their sides.

f: What are the two preliminary points clarified regarding the position of the hands in prayer?
b:
1. All positions mentioned in the hadiths are permissible, and the difference of opinion only concerns which is the most preferable method. 

2. There are very few rigorously authenticated (sahih) hadiths concerning this issue; most reports explaining the different ways have been classified as extremely weak or slightly defective.

f: What is the first difference of opinion concerning the positioning of the hands in prayer?
b: Whether the hands should be clasped together or not. Imam Malik's more popular opinion (related by Ibn al-Qasim) is that hands should be left hanging at the sides, while his second view (related by Ibn al-Mundhir) is that they should be brought together and placed on the body.

f: What is the consensus of the majority of scholars regarding whether hands should be clasped or left hanging at the sides?
b: Imam Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, Imam Shafi'i, Imam Ahmad, and the majority of scholars are of the opinion that the hands should be clasped together and not left to hang at the side. As the Maliki scholar Ibn 'Abd al-Barr states, there is nothing reported from the Messenger ﷺ contradicting this majority opinion, and it is the unanimous view of all Companions and Followers (tabi'in) (Awjaz al-masalik 2:116).

f: What reasons and reports exist regarding leaving the hands at the sides?
b: Scholars note there are no authentic hadiths substantiating Imam Malik's opinion of leaving hands at the sides. Some mention the reason may be profound fear, awe, and reverence for Allah causing a person standing before Him to forget bringing their hands together. Regardless, reports of some Companions praying with their hands on their sides can be found (Musannaf Ibn Abi Shayba 2:391).

f: What is the second difference of opinion regarding the hands in prayer, and what are the specific views of the major imams?
b:
The difference is over where on the body hands should be positioned after clasping: 

• Imam Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Abu Ishaq al-Marwazi (Shafi'i): Positioned below the navel. 

• Imam Shafi'i: Most popular view (in al-Wasit and Kitab al-Umm) is beneath the chest; a second opinion (in al-Hawi) is directly on the chest. 

• Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal: Three opinions—first (more popular, similar to Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ) is beneath the navel; second is similar to Shafi'i (on the chest); third is that a person has the choice of either placing them beneath the navel or on the chest since both are derived from the Sunna.

f: Why is the narration of Wa'il ibn Hujr ؓ considered problematic (mudtarib) and inconsistent by scholars?
b:
Because different versions vary greatly on where the hands were placed: 

• Sahih Ibn Khuzayma: "I performed prayer with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He placed his right hand upon the left one on his chest." 

• Musnad al-Bazzar: States "near his chest" instead of "upon his chest". 

• Musannaf Ibn Abi Shayba: States "beneath the navel." 

All three versions contain some type of weakness.

f: Why is the first version of Wa'il ibn Hujr's narration (found in Sahih Ibn Khuzayma containing "upon his chest") considered the weakest?
b:
• Mu'ammal ibn Isma'il: A weak narrator who erred after his books were buried and he narrated from memory. Imam Bukhari called him munkar al-hadith ("His narrations are rejected"), 'Allama Dhahabi said "He makes many errors" (kathir al-khata'), and Abu Zur'a noted his narrations contain many errors (Fath al-Mulhim 2:40). 

• Lack of corroboration: Other versions in Sunan Abi Dawud, Nasa'i, Ibn Maja, and Musnad Abi Dawud al-Tayalisi رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ do not contain the addition "on the chest" (Allama Nimawi). 

• Broken link: Hafiz ibn Hajar al-'Asqalani stated the link between Mu'ammal and Sufyan al-Thawri is weak (Fath al-Bari 206 U). 

• Contradiction with narrator's view: Sufyan al-Thawri himself was of the opinion that hands should be positioned beneath the navel; under usul al-hadith, a narrator's narration in contradiction to his personal opinion is not accepted. 

• Not all of Ibn Khuzayma is authentic: Allama Suyuti noted in Tadrib al-rawi that Sahih Ibn Khuzayma contains some weak and munkar reports. 

• Imam Tirmidhi's silence: Tirmidhi made no comment regarding its authenticity, showing it is not rigorously authenticated. 

• Isolated practice (shadh): Even if accepted, placing hands on the chest would be considered an isolated practice done a few times solely to inform of its permissibility (bayanan li 'l-jawaz), not a permanent practice.

f: Why is the second version of Wa'il ibn Hujr's narration (found in Musnad al-Bazzar containing "near the chest") rejected?
b: One of its narrators is Muhammad ibn Hujr, regarding whom Imam Bukhari stated, "His matter is unsettled," and 'Allama Dhahabi stated, "Some of his narrations are rejected" (Majma' al-zawa'id 2:135).

f: What is the issue with the narration of Hulb ؓ transmitted by Imam Ahmad regarding placing the hand on the chest?
b: 'Allama Nimawi established with convincing evidence that there is a copyist error in the wording: instead of 'ala badhihi ("upon the other hand"), the copyist mistakenly wrote 'ala sadrihi ("on his chest") (Athar al-sunan 87).

f: What does the Hanafi explanation state regarding the various narrations of the Messenger ﷺ placing his hands on his chest or just below it?
b: The Hanafis explain that the Messenger ﷺ did, at one time or another, place his hands on his chest or just below it only to demonstrate the permissibility of such a posture (bayanan li 'l-jawaz), whereas his normal and routine practice was to place his hands below his navel.

f: What is the status of the third version of Wa'il ibn Hujr's narration mentioning "below the navel"?
b:
• Some Hanafi scholars noted it cannot be used as conclusive evidence because the words "below the navel" are only found in some editions of Musannaf Ibn Abi Shayba (and not an inconsistent text). 

• However, 'Allama Qasim ibn Qutlubgah judged it to be of sound transmission, 'Allama Muhammad Abu 'l-Tayyib al-Madani wrote it has a strong chain, and Shaykh 'Abid Sindhi stated its narrators are trustworthy (Athar al-sunan 148). 

• Despite its problematic nature, it cannot be rendered totally unacceptable due to many other reliable reports strengthening it.

f: What is reported from 'Ali رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ regarding placing hands below the navel, and what is the evaluation of its chain?
b:
• 'Ali رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ stated: "To place one palm over the other beneath the navel is from the sunna acts of prayer" (Sunan al-Bayhaqi 312 U, Musannaf Ibn Abi Shayba 1:391). 

• When a Companion says "It is from the Sunna," it is a known fact that it is acquired from the Messenger ﷺ himself. 

• The chain contains 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ishaq, who has been classified as weak; however, because other reliable narrations reinforce it, the Hanafis use it as supplementary evidence.

f: What are the narrations from Hajjaj ibn al-Hasan and Ibrahim al-Nakh'ay رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ regarding hand placement?
b:
• Hajjaj ibn al-Hasan: Asked Abu Mijlaz about hand position, who replied: "He should place the inner portion of his right hand upon the back of the left one beneath the navel" (Musannaf Ibn Abi Shayba 1:390), with a sound (hasan) transmission according to 'Allama Ibn al-Turkumani al-Mardini. 

• Ibrahim al-Nakh'ay رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ: States "One should place his right hand upon the left one beneath the navel while in prayer" (Musannaf Ibn Abi Shayba 1:390), also with a sound (hasan) transmission.

f: What are the reports from Abu Hurayra رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ and Anas رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ regarding hand placement beneath the navel?
b:
• Abu Hurayra رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ: Narrates that "The placing of one hand over the other in prayer should be beneath the navel" (al-Jawhar al-naqi 2:31 U). 

• Anas رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ: Reports that "there are three aspects from the characteristics of prophethood [nubuwwa]: to open fast early; to delay the predawn meal [suhur]; and to position the right hand over the left one beneath the navel while in prayer" (al-Jawhar al-naqi 2:31 U).

f: What reasoning does the great Hanafi jurist Ibn al-Humam provide for placing hands beneath the navel?
b: Due to inconsistencies and contradictions in various narrations, it is best to resort to analogy and reasoning. Standing before the Lord demands a posture expressing respect and reverence; positioning hands beneath the navel is the most respectful and superior way of standing. Additionally, women are instructed to place hands on their chests for greater concealment and modesty (Fath al-Qadir).

f: What does 'Allama Badr al-Din 'Ayni write in 'Umdat al-Qari regarding positioning hands beneath the navel?
b:
1. It holds great virtue, signifies great respect, and displays greater contrast to the postures of disbelievers. 

2. It is the same posture in which one stands before worldly rulers. 

3. Placing hands on the chest creates a similarity with women, hence it cannot be classified as the sunna for men ('Umdat al-Qari 3:16 U).

f: What is the chapter's final conclusion regarding hand placement in prayer?
b: Although hadiths from various schools contain some weakness, the Hanafi reports have received less criticism and have stronger reports to supplement weaker ones. Hadiths for placing hands on or below the chest do not denote the normal practice of the Messenger ﷺ, who Hanafis agree sometimes placed them on/below the chest only to show permissibility (bayanan li 'l-jawaz). Placing hands beneath the navel exhibits greater respect and humility, and just as other prayer postures differ between males and females, hand positioning differs as well.

f: Why is the issue of reciting behind the imam (qira'a khalF al-imam) considered so serious and controversial?
b: Because the debate is not just about which method is superior or more virtuous, but concerns the actual permissibility—whether reciting Surat al-Fatiha behind the imam is wajib (necessary) or totally forbidden (haram).

f: What points of agreement exist among scholars regarding recitation in prayer?
b:
1. All scholars agree that it is obligatory (fard) on the imam and the person praying by himself (munfarid) to recite Surat al-Fatiha. 

2. They agree the muqtadi (follower) is exempted from reciting anything beyond Surat al-Fatiha, whereas the imam and munfarid must recite at least a few short verses/small chapter in the first two rak'ats of fard prayers and all rak'ats of non-fard prayers.

f: What are the views of Imam Malik and Imam Ahmad regarding the follower reciting Surat al-Fatiha?
b: They are of the view that the follower is not required to recite Surat al-Fatiha in the audible (jahri) prayer, but is required to do so in the silent (sirri) prayers. Imam Malik stated it is undesirable (makruh) for the follower to recite in audible prayers (Fath al-Mulhim 2:20).

f: How did Imam Shafi'i's view on recitation behind the imam evolve between his popular view and his later book Al-Umm?
b:
• Popular/Former view: Necessary for the follower in both audible and silent prayers (al-Mughni 1:601). 

• Later view (Kitab al-Umm 7:153 U): Not necessary for the muqtadi to recite Surat al-Fatiha in audible prayers, but should be recited in silent prayers ("And we say that the follower should recite in every prayer performed behind an imam in which the imam recites in a non-audible tone"). (Confirmed as his later work by Hafiz Ibn Kathir and 'Allama Suyuti).

f: What is the view of Dawud al-Zahiri عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ and Imam Ibn Taymiyya regarding reciting Surat al-Fatiha in audible prayers?
b: They were of the view that Surat al-Fatiha should not be recited in the audible prayers (making the view that it is fard in audible prayers an isolated and unique position).

f: What is the unanimous position of the Hanafi Imams (Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, Abu Yusuf رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, and Imam Muhammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ) regarding recitation by the follower?
b: They state it is forbidden (haram)—though it does not nullify the prayer—for the follower to recite any portion of the Qur'an (whether Fatiha or another verse) in both silent and audible prayers behind the imam; the imam's recitation is sufficient for the follower.

f: What Qur'anic verse is presented as proof by the Hanafi school that no recitation should be undertaken by the follower?
b:
Allah says in the Qur'an:

"So, when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it, and remain silent, that you may receive mercy" (Al-Qur'an 7:204). 

The text notes this verse is sufficient proof that no recitation whatsoever should be...

f: According to Tanzim al-ashtat (commentary of Mishkat al-Masabih), what two commands does verse 7:204 give to the follower?
b:
1. To remain completely silent—which relates to both silent and audible prayers. 

2. To listen with concentration—which relates only to audible prayers.

f: How do Hafiz Ibn Taymiya and Imam Qudama (al-Mughni) counter the claim that verse 7:204 was revealed regarding the Friday sermon (khutba) only?
b:
• Ibn Taymiya: Pious predecessors (salaf salih) understood it was revealed concerning prayer (though some said sermon), and Imam Ahmad reported a consensus among scholars that it was revealed concerning prayer (Majmu' al-fatawa 23:269). 

• Imam Qudama: Imam Ahmad stated after a report of Abu Dawud, "The people are unanimous that this verse was revealed concerning the prayer" (1:601). Furthermore, it is a Makkan verse, whereas the Friday prayer and sermon only became obligatory later in Madina.

f: What narration is related from the great exegete Mujahid regarding the revelation of verse 7:204?
b: Both Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Imam Bayhaqi related a hadith from Mujahid that: "This verse was revealed concerning some Companions of the Messenger ﷺ reciting behind the imam". Even though it is mursal, Mujahid is known as a'lam al-nas bi 'l-tafsir (one of the greatest exegetes), so his mursal reports are accepted.

f: What report is related by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari from Yasir ibn Jabir regarding 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud ؓ?
b: 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud ؓ heard a few people reciting with the imam during prayer. Upon completing his prayer, he remarked: "Has the time not come for you to understand? Has the time not come for you to realize that when the Qur'an is being recited, you must listen to it attentively and remain silent just as Allah has ordered you to?" (I'la' al-sunan 4:43, Tafsir al-Tabari 11:378).

f: What is the Hanafi distinction between fard and wajib regarding obligations and the consequences of neglecting them?
b:
• Fard: Established through decisive proof (dalil qat'i); neglecting it renders the entire prayer invalid, and it cannot be compensated by prostrations of forgetfulness. 

• Wajib: Established through speculative proof (dalil zanni); neglecting it renders the prayer deficient (not entirely invalid) and can be compensated through the prostrations of forgetfulness (sajdat al-sahw).

f: How do the Hanafis derive that reciting any portion of the Qur'an is fard and reciting Surat al-Fatiha is wajib?
b:
• They derive that reciting any portion of the Qur'an is fard based on verse 73:20 ("So recite as much of the Qur'an as may be easy for you"), treating ma as a general ('am) term encompassing the whole Qur'an. 

• Based on the hadith "There is no prayer except with Surat al-Fatiha," they render the recital of Surat al-Fatiha specifically to be wajib. Thus, the imam and munfarid must recite Fatiha with other verses, while the muqtadi does not recite at all because they are commanded to remain silent.

f: What were the circumstances of revelation for verse 17:110 ("And say your prayer neither aloud nor in a low voice...") according to Ibn 'Abbas رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا?
b: It was revealed when the Messenger ﷺ was discreetly inviting people to Islam in Makka and recited aloud in prayer. When polytheistic mushrikin heard his recitation, they would revile the Holy Qur'an, Allah, and the Prophet ﷺ. Thus, Allah instructed: "And say your prayer neither aloud... but make it so that the believers can hear you" (Al-Ta'liq al-sabih 1:366, Sahih Muslim).

f: What are the full texts of Hadiths 1 and 2 (narrated by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ and Abu Hurayra رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ) regarding remaining silent behind the imam?
b:
• Hadith 1 (Abu Sa'id al-Khudri ؓ): "The Messenger ﷺ delivered a sermon in which he outlined our Way [Sunna] for us and taught us our prayer. He instructed, 'When you prepare for prayer, straighten your rows; then one of you [should become the imam to] lead the others in prayer. When he proclaims the takbir you also proclaim it; when he recites remain silent; and when he reaches "ghayr al-maghdubi 'alayhim wala 'l-dallin," say "amin," and Allah will answer your prayer' (Sahih Muslim 1:174)". 

• Hadith 2 (Abu Hurayra ؓ): "The imam has been assigned to be followed. When he proclaims the takbir you also proclaim it; when he recites remain silent; and when he says "sami' Allahu liman hamidah," say "Rabbana laka 'l-hamd" (Sunan Abi Dawud 1:96, Sunan al-Nasa'i 46)".

f: What key deductions are drawn from Hadith 1 and 2 regarding amin and following the imam?
b:
1. Purpose of Amin: The follower says amin ("O Allah, accept") to endorse the du'a' made by the imam at the end of Fatiha. If followers were required to recite Fatiha themselves, they would say amin at the end of their own recitations, but the Prophet ﷺ ordered it said collectively upon the imam's completion. 

2. Meaning of "assigned to be followed": The follower must remain silent to listen to the imam's recitation; reciting on one's own while the imam recites would be rude and makes attentive listening impossible.

f: What are the narrations of Jabir رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ and the Messenger ﷺ (Hadiths 3 & 4) regarding the sufficiency of the imam's recitation?
b:
• Jabir رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ (Hadith 3): "whoever prays behind an imam, his imam's recitation is sufficient for him (al-Jawhar al-naqi 2:159, I'la' al-sunan 4:61, Musannaf Ibn Abi Shayba 1:377)". 

• The Messenger ﷺ (Hadith 4): "Whoever prays behind the imam, his imam's recitation is sufficient for him ('Umdat al-qari 3:12, Muwatta Muhammad 96, I'la' al-sunan 4:61)".

f: What are the details of Hadith 5 ('Abdullah ibn Shaddad) and Hadith 6 regarding recitation behind the imam?
b:
• Hadith 5 ('Abdullah ibn Shaddad): The Messenger ﷺ led the 'Asr prayer. A person began reciting behind him, so the person next to him gave him a nudge. After finishing prayer, the person asked, "Why did you nudge me?" The other replied, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in front of you, and I did not approve of you reciting behind him." The Messenger ﷺ heard this and said, "Whoever has an imam, the recitation of the imam is sufficient for him" (Muwatta Imam Muhammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ 98, I'la' al-sunan 4:70). 

• Hadith 6: Someone asked the Messenger ﷺ: "O Messenger of Allah ﷺ! Is there recitation in every prayer?" The Messenger ﷺ said yes. Somebody asked, "[Does that mean] it is necessary?" The Messenger ﷺ replied, "I consider the imam's recitation to be sufficient [for the muqtadi]" (Majma' al-zawa'id 2:110).

f: How does Ibn Taymiya summarize the legal ruling on the sufficiency of the imam's recitation in his Fatawa?
b: "The recitation of the imam is sufficient for the muqtadi. The consensus of the Companions and the Followers proves this. The hadiths from which this [rule] is established are narrated without any Companion being omitted from the transmission [musnadan], as well as some with the Companion being omitted from the transmission [mursalan]. The legal rulings [fatawa] among the Followers were also that the [imam's] recitation is sufficient. Above all, it is in total accordance with the Qur'an and Sunna (Majmu' al-fatawa 23:271)".

f: What is reported in Hadith 7 (Abu Hurayra ؓ), Hadith 8 ('Imran ibn Husayn ؓ), and Hadith 9 ('Abdullah ibn Mas'ud ؓ) regarding the Prophet's ﷺ disapproval of reciting behind him?
b:
• Hadith 7 (Abu Hurayra ؓ): After an audible salat, the Messenger ﷺ asked, "Did one of you recite with me?" A person replied, "Yes, O Messenger of Allah ﷺ." The Messenger ﷺ remarked, "I was wondering why I felt as if the words of the Qur'an were being taken from my tongue" (Sunan al-Tirmidhi 1:71, Muwatta Imam Malik 51, Sunan al-Nasa'i 1:146, Sunan Abi Dawud 1:146, Sunan Ibn Maja 61, Sunan al-Bayhaqi 2:157). Upon hearing this, people discontinued reciting behind him during audible prayers. 

• Hadith 8 ('Imran ibn Husayn ؓ): During Zuhr, a person recited Sabbihi isma rabbik al-a'la behind the Prophet ﷺ. Afterward, the Prophet ﷺ asked who recited it and remarked, "I thought one of you was taking it [the verses] from my tongue" (Sahih Muslim 1:172, I'la' al-sunan 4:56). 

• Hadith 9 ('Abdullah ibn Mas'ud ؓ): The Companions would recite behind the Messenger ﷺ. Once he said to them, "You have caused me confusion in my recitation of the Qur'an" (Majma' al-zawa'id 2:110, al-Jawhar al-naqi 1:162).

f: What are the reports from 'Ata' ibn Yasar and Nafi'/'Abdullah ibn 'Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا regarding recitation behind the imam?
b:
• 'Ata' ibn Yasar: Enquired from Zayd ibn Thabit ؓ regarding recitation behind the imam; he said, "There is no recitation behind the imam" (Sahih Muslim 1:215). 

• Nafi' reporting from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا: When asked if anything should be recited behind the imam, he replied: "Whenever one of you prays behind the imam, the recitation of the imam is sufficient for him; but when you pray alone, you should recite for yourself." The narrator notes 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا would not recite behind the imam (Muwatta Imam Malik 51, I'la' al-sunan 4:76).

f: What did 'Ubaydullah ibn Muqsim learn when he enquired from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا, Zayd ibn Thabit, and Jabir ibn 'Abdillah رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ?
b: They informed him that there should be no recitation behind the imam in any prayer (Athar al-sunan 1:116, I'la' al-sunan 4:81).

f: How did 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Abu Jamra express their views on reciting behind the imam?
b:
• 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: Expressed great disapproval, saying, "Would that the mouth of the person reciting behind the imam be filled with dust" (Athar al-sunan 1:116, I'la' al-sunan 4:81). 

• Abu Jamra: Asked Ibn 'Abbas رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا, "Should I recite when the imam is in front of me?" He said no (Athar al-sunan 1:116, I'la' al-sunan 4:81).

f: What did Ibn 'Abbas رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا narrate from the Messenger ﷺ regarding the imam's recitation?
b: That the recitation of the imam is sufficient for the muqtadi, whether he recites silently or aloud (Daraqutni 1:331, I'la' al-sunan 4:82).

f: What do the statements of Musa ibn 'Uqba عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ, Musa ibn Sa'id عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ, Ibrahim al-Nakh'ay رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, and Muhammad ibn Sirin state regarding recitation behind the imam?
b:
• Musa ibn 'Uqba عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ: Reports that the Messenger ﷺ, Abu Bakr رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, 'Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, and 'Uthman رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ would forbid reciting behind the imam (Umdat al-qari 3:67 U, I'la' al-sunan 4:84). 

• Musa ibn Sa'id ibn Zayd ibn Thabit رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ (from Zayd ibn Thabit): "Whoever recites behind the imam, there is no prayer for him" (Muwatta Imam Muhammad رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ 100, I'la' al-sunan 4:87). 

• Ibrahim al-Nakh'ay رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ: "The first thing the people innovated [in religion] was recitation behind the imam—the Companions did not recite behind the imam" (al-Jawhar al-naqi 4:169). 

• Muhammad ibn Sirin: "I do not consider reciting behind the imam to be from the Sunna" (Musannaf Ibn Abi Shayba 1:377, I'la' al-sunan 4:90).

f: Which ten Companions are reported by 'Abdullah ibn Zayd ibn Aslam to have strongly prohibited reciting behind the imam?
b: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, 'Umar al-Faruq رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Zayd ibn Thabit, 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا, and 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas (Qala'id al-azhar 2:42 U).

f: What statements were made by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ, Sa'd ؓ, and 'Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ regarding the invalidity or prohibition of reciting behind the imam?
b:
• 'Ali ibn Abi Talib رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ: "Whoever recites behind the imam, his prayer is not valid," and in another narration: "[...] such a person has deviated from the natural path [fitra]" (al-Jawhar al-naqi 2:218, Musannaf Ibn Abi Shayba 1:376). 

• Sa'd: "I desire that a burning ember be placed in the mouth of one who recites behind the imam" (Musannaf 'Abd al-Razzaq 2:138, Musannaf Ibn Abi Shayba 2:376). 

• 'Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ: "Would that there be a stone in the mouth of one who recites behind the imam" (Musannaf 'Abd al-Razzaq 2:128).

f: What are the four primary reasons/rationales provided for not reciting behind the imam?
b:
1. Concentration & Audible Recitation: The imam recites aloud so followers listen in total silence; if followers recited as well, they could not concentrate on the imam's recitation, forcing the imam to recite aloud to a congregation not required to listen. 

2. Representation in Du'a': Surat al-Fatiha contains a du'a' (invocation for guidance); just as a group appointing a single representative to speak or submit a proposal does so without interference from members, the imam makes the du'a' on behalf of the entire congregation, who endorse it by saying amin. 

3. Late Arrivals in Ruku': If someone arrives late and joins the imam directly in bowing (ruku'), they still acquire that rak'a even though they missed the standing posture (qiyam) and reciting Fatiha, proving Fatiha is not fard on the muqtadi since the imam's recitation is sufficient. 

4. Congregational Commonalities: When an imam makes a mistake, the whole congregation performs sajdat al-sahw with him; when he recites a "verse of prostration," the congregation performs sajda even if recited silently; a single sutra in front of the imam is sufficient for the whole congregation. Thus, the imam's recitation being sufficient follows this same communal principle.

f: What are the two narrations of 'Ubada ibn al-Samit regarding recitation in prayer, and how do scholars generally view them?
b:
• Narrations: 1) "There is no prayer for the one who does not recite Surat al-Fatiha" (Sahih Muslim); 2) "There is no prayer for the one who does not recite Surat al-Fatiha and [some] more [verses]" (Sahih Muslim). 

• Status: Classified as rigorously authenticated (sahih), they are typically presented as evidence that reciting Fatiha is fard on the muqtadi.

f: What are the five explanations (a–e) provided by scholars/Hanafi texts to reconcile 'Ubada ibn al-Samit's narration with the Hanafi position?
b:
(a) Both imam and muqtadi are obligated, but the follower's obligation is fulfilled through the imam's recitation since the Messenger ﷺ stated the imam's recitation is sufficient for the muqtadi. 

(b) The hadith concerns the imam and the person praying by himself only, as followers are commanded in the Qur'an to remain silent and listen. 

(c) Rigorously authenticated hadiths totally prohibit the follower from reciting behind the imam; thus, in view of those prohibitions, this hadith is directed at the imam and lone worshipper. 

(d) The second narration includes "and more" (fasa'idan). Since everyone agrees that reciting extra verses is not fard on the follower (its obligation being absolved by the imam's recitation), the exact same reasoning applies to Surat al-Fatiha. 

(e) The obligation of Surat al-Fatiha is directed at the imam and the person praying alone only.

f: What statement of Jabir رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ with a reliable transmission is narrated in Sunan al-Tirmidhi (1:71)?
b:
"Whoever performed a rak'a in which he did not recite Surat al-Fatiha, is as though he has not performed it, unless he was [praying] behind the imam" (Sunan al-Tirmidhi 1:71). 

Explanation: Imam Tirmidhi noted Imam Ahmad explained that Jabir رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ (a Companion) interpreted the general statement to apply only when praying by oneself.

f: What are the details of the second narration of 'Ubada ibn al-Samit regarding the Fajr prayer (Sunan Abi Dawud, Tirmidhi, Nasa'i)?
b: During Fajr behind the Messenger ﷺ, the Prophet ﷺ experienced difficulty reciting. Upon finishing, he asked, "Perhaps you were reciting behind your imam?" When they replied yes, he said, "Do not recite anything besides Surat al-Fatiha, for there is no prayer for the one who does not recite it". A narration in Sunan Abi Dawud adds: "I was wondering why the words of the Qur'an were being taken from my tongue. Do not recite any portion of the Qur'an while I am reciting aloud, except Surat al-Fatiha".

f: Why do scholars state that the apparent wording allowing Fatiha in the second narration cannot be taken literally or is set aside?
b:
(a) Weak narrator in chain: Muhammad ibn Ishaq is present; while some considered him trustworthy, major critics like Sulayman al-Taymi عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ, Hisham, and Imam Malik called him a "flagrant liar" (kadhdhab / dajjalun min al-dajajila), alongside severe criticisms from Ibn Zahir, Daraqutni, and others. 

(b) Confusion in transmission (mudtarib): Makhul relates it sometimes from Muhammad ibn Rabi', sometimes from Nafi' ibn Mahmud (whom experts like Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, Tahawi, and Ibn Qudama state is "unknown" / majhul). 

(c) Defective (ma'lul / mu'allal): Hadith experts classified it as defective because its transmission reached only 'Ubada ibn al-Samit (mawquf) rather than the Prophet ﷺ (marfu'), as explained by Ibn Taymiya and Imam Ahmad.

f: What further explanation does Imam Tirmidhi give regarding the transmission of 'Ubada ibn al-Samit's narration about Fajr prayer?
b: Imam Tirmidhi notes that the actual authenticated (sahih) narration of the Messenger ﷺ in this regard is simply "There is no prayer without the Umm al-Quran," transmitted in Sahihayn via Zuhri from 'Ubada ؓ through Muhammad ibn Rabi'. However, some narrators from al-Sham (Levant) erred, as 'Ubada ؓ was the Imam of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) when he related this, and they confused his own statement (mawquf) as being related directly from the Messenger ﷺ (marfu'). Thus, the addition is inadmissible as evidence.

f: How do Hanafis interpret the phrase "iqra' ha fi nafsik" ("recite it in your mind") from Abu Hurayra's رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ narration?
b:
1. It means "recite it in your mind and ponder over it, and do not utter it with your tongue," allowing the muqtadi to concentrate on the imam's recitation. 

2. It could be translated as "Recite it when you are performing prayer individually," supported by a hadith qudsi stating: "If the servant remembers Me while he is alone [fi nafsi], I remember him similarly [fi nafsi]; and if he remembers Me in a gathering, then I remember him in a gathering more superior to his". Since the opposite of being in a gathering is being alone, the meaning is to recite Surat al-Fatiha when praying alone, not in congregation.

f: What virtue and ruling are associated with saying amin after Surat al-Fatiha, and what does the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari (1:108) state?
b:
• Virtue & Ruling: Saying amin ("aameen") holds great virtue and is a sunna of the Prophet ﷺ; all scholars are unanimous that it is sunna to say it at that time. 

• Hadith (Sahih al-Bukhari 1:108): "When the imam says 'ghayr al-maghdubi 'alayhim wala 'l-dallin,' say amin, because the angels say amin. And whoever's amin coincides with the amin of the angels, all his past sins are forgiven".

f: What is the nature of the difference of opinion regarding saying amin audibly or silently, according to Ibn al-Qayyim (Zad al-ma'ad 1:70)?
b: The difference of opinion is solely about which method is superior (audible vs. silent). Ibn al-Qayyim notes it is among valid differences where no criticism should be directed at those who say it aloud or silently, comparing it to the issue of raising hands (raf' al-yadayn).

f: What are the different opinions of the schools regarding whether amin should be said audibly or silently?
b:
• Hanafi Opinion: Amin should be said inaudibly at all times; the Prophet ﷺ said it aloud only a few times to familiarize Companions, after which he said it silently like all other invocations. 

• Another Group: Should be said aloud in all audible prayers (Fajr, Maghrib, 'Isha) and silently in silent prayers (Zuhr, 'Asr). 

• Imam Malik and Imam Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ: The imam should say amin silently in silent prayers, and followers should always say amin silently in both audible and silent prayers (an opinion also shared by Imam Shafi'i). 

• Another Group: Followers should say amin audibly during audible prayers and silently during silent prayers. 

(Note: Saying amin aloud or silently is regarded by all as a sunna act, not a fard).

f: How do scholars explain that amin is a du'a (invocation), referencing Sura Yunus (10:89) and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah (Sahih al-Bukhari 1:102)?
b:
• Definition: Amin is a verbal noun meaning "accept [our] prayer," making it a du'a. 

• Sura Yunus (10:89): Regarding "Accepted is your prayer (O Musa عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ and Harun)!," the dual tense ("da'watukuma") is used even though only Musa عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ made the du'a and Harun endorsed it with amin. Ibn Mardawayh relates via Anas رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ that Musa عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ made the du'a and Harun said amin (Fath al-Bari). 

• 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah: Quoted by Imam Bukhari in Sahih al-Bukhari (1:102) as saying, "Amin is a du'a". 

• Etiquette: Since it is a du'a, it follows the etiquette taught by Allah: "Invoke your Lord with humility and in secret. He likes not the aggressors" (Al-Qur'an 7:55).

f: How do Qur'anic verses (e.g., 13:3, 21:90, 20:108) support the position that amin should be said silently?
b:
• Allah commands making prayers and du'as with humility, sincerity, and in silence (khufya). 

• Zakariyya's invocation was "a call in secret" (13:3). 

• Envoys "used to call on Us with hope and fear" (21:90). 

• On the Last Day, "you shall hear nothing but the low sound of their footsteps" (20:108). 

Since amin is a du'a, it should be said silently like other du'as, matching the teachings that Allah is Near and All-Hearing and does not require loud invocation.

f: What is mentioned in the narration of Samura ibn Jundub and 'Imran ibn Husayn ؓ regarding the Prophet's ﷺ silences (sakta)?
b:
• Samura related two occasions of short silence in prayer: one following the initial takbir and the second when completing wala 'l-dallin. 

• 'Imran ibn Husayn initially wrote to Ubay bin Ka'b because he couldn't acknowledge this; Ubay replied that Samura remembered correctly (Sunan Abi Dawud 1:120). 

• Commenting on this, 'Allama Nimawi states the first silence was to recite thana silently, and the second was to say amin silently. 'Imran likely refuted the second silence because it was so brief and he didn't think it worthy of mention, acknowledging the longer first silence. This proves amin was recited during the second silence (Athar al-sunan 382).

f: How does the narration of Abu Hurayra رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ (Sunan al-Nasa'i 1:147) indicate that the imam should say amin silently?
b: The Prophet ﷺ instructed: "When the imam recites 'ghayr al-maghdubi 'alayhim wala 'l-dallin,' say amin, because the angels say it and so does the imam". If it were preferable for the imam to say it aloud, there would be no reason for the Prophet ﷺ to inform the Companions that the imam also says amin, because they would have heard it themselves. Informing them means it was normally said in a subdued tone.

f: What are the two differing reports from Shu'ba and Sufyan al-Thawri regarding Wa'il ibn Hujr's ؓ narration about saying amin?
b:
• Shu'ba's narration: When the Prophet ﷺ reached wala 'l-dallin, he said amin and kept his voice subdued (Musnad Ahmad, Daraqutni, al-Mustadrak U, Nasb al-raya 1:494). 

• Sufyan's narration: The Prophet ﷺ prolonged his voice (madda biha sawtahu) while saying amin (Sunan al-Tirmidhi 1:57, Abi Dawud 1:142). 

• Hanafi/Scholarly Reconciling: While critics favor Sufyan's report to claim amin was said aloud, Hanafis explain that Sufyan's report means the initial vowel (alif) of amin was prolonged (elongated) rather than the volume of the voice being raised, a position supported and defended in works like Athar al-sunan and Fath al-Mulhim.

f: How do Hanafis interpret Abu Hurayra's رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ narration ("When the imam says amin, you say it") (Sahih al-Bukhari 1:108)?
b: If it were preferable to say amin aloud, the wording would have read "When the imam says amin, you say it" using the imam's audible amin as the direct signal. However, because the Prophet ﷺ instructed them to say amin after the imam recited wala 'l-dallin, it shows the imam's amin was pronounced silently. Occasional narrations saying "When the imam says amin..." are interpreted as "When the time comes for the imam to say amin..." rather than literally, since his normal practice was to say it silently.

f: What do the reports from early Companions and Followers (Abu Wa'il, Ibrahim al-Nakh'ay رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ) state regarding bismillah, ta'awwudh, and amin?
b:
• Abu Wa'il: 'Ali رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ and 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud ؓ did not recite bismillah, a'udhu bi'llah, or amin aloud (Majma' al-zawa'id 2:108); 'Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ and 'Ali رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ would also not recite them aloud (I'la' al-sunan 2:215). 

• Ibrahim al-Nakh'ay رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ (Musannaf 'Abd al-Razzaq 2:87): Stated there are five things the imam should say silently: subhanaka 'llahumma (thana), ta'awwudh, bismillah, amin, and Allahumma rabbana laka 'l-hamd.

f: What additional reasons are provided for saying amin silently?
b:
1. Avoiding Confusion with the Qur'an: Quranic recitation must be audible in audible prayers; saying amin aloud could mislead people into assuming it is part of the Qur'an alongside Fatiha, whereas all scholars agree amin is not part of the Qur'an. 

2. Analogy to Bismillah: Some scholars consider bismillah a verse of Surat al-Fatiha yet do not recite it aloud during prayer, proving that invocations like amin (which no scholar considers part of the Qur'an) should definitely not be said aloud.

f: How do Hanafis answer the narration of Abu Hurayra رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ (Sunan Abi Dawud) stating that amin was heard in the first row, including the version in Sunan Ibn Maja (1:61) about the masjid echoing?
b:
1. Weak narrator: One of its narrators is Bishr ibn Rafi', who has been strongly criticized by hadith experts—Imam Bukhari stated "He is not consistent in his narrations," Imam Ahmad called him weak, Imam Nasa'i stated "He is not strong," and Ibn Hibban stated "He relates spurious narrations" (Mizan al-i'tidal U). 

2. Self-contradictory: It is unclear how one version states it was heard from the first row only, while the other states the whole masjid echoed. Thus, the hadith is self-contradictory and cannot be accepted as evidence.

f: How do scholars (like Ibn al-Qayyim, Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, and Hafiz Abu Bishr al-Dulabi) reconcile the differing reports regarding saying amin aloud vs. silently?
b:
• General reconciliation: The Prophet ﷺ said amin aloud only for a short period of time to emphasize its importance and teach the Companions, similar to 'Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ reciting thana aloud for a few days before continuing silently, or 'Abbas reciting Fatiha during funeral prayer to teach it (Zad al-ma'ad 1:70). 

• Wa'il ibn Hujr's statement: Transmitted by Hafiz Abu Bishr al-Dulabi: "I do not think the Messenger ﷺ said it [amin] aloud except to teach us" (Athar al-sunan 93, Fath al-Mulhim 2:50-52). 

• Ibn Jarir al-Tabari: Both types of reports are reliable/authentic (sahih), referring to different occasions—silent reports reflect his normal, permanent practice, while audible reports reflect rare instances to teach the Companions.

f: What points are raised regarding the frequency of prayer and the scarcity of reports supporting audible amin?
b: There are five prayers a day. If amin were said aloud in three of them permanently, it would have been widely reported by many Companions rather than just a few. Wa'il ibn Hujr, who lived in Yemen, visited Madinah only a few times, so the Prophet ﷺ likely said it aloud in his presence solely to teach him (as Wa'il himself noted: "I do not think the Messenger ﷺ said it aloud except to teach us"). Furthermore, Wa'il's narration in Sunan al-Nasa'i (1:147 U) states: "When the Messenger ﷺ recited 'ghayr al-maghdubi 'alayhim wala 'l-dallin,' he said amin. I heard him [say it] since I was behind him," indicating he only heard it because he was directly behind him, not because it was pronounced loudly.

f: What is the nature of the difference of opinion regarding raising the hands (raf' al-yadayn) in prayer, and is it a matter of fard or haram?
b: It is not a debate about something being obligatory (fard) or unlawful (haram), but merely a difference in ascertaining the better of two ways (which method is more virtuous). Both methods are permissible according to most scholars, as both are derived from hadiths.

f: What are the three main positions regarding raising the hands at various points in the prayer?
b:
1. Opening takbir (tahrima): All scholars are unanimous that hands should be raised at this point. 

2. Before and after bowing (ruku'): One group states it is sunna and more virtuous to raise hands; another group (including Imam Malik and Imam Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ) holds that it is sunna and preferable not to raise hands at these instances. 

3. Moving into prostration (sajda) or returning to third standing (qiyam): All scholars of Ahl al-Sunna are unanimous that it is no longer sunna to raise hands at these instances, as that practice was abrogated.

f: What regional practices (ta'amul) of the three great early Islamic cities (Madina, Makka, and Kufa) shaped the juristic views on raf' al-yadayn?
b:
• Madina (Imam Malik): Based his opinion on the continuous practice of the people of Madina who did not observe raising the hands after the opening takbir. As stated in al-Mudawwana: "I do not consider the raising of the hands to be part of any takbir of the prayer... except at the beginning of prayer" (al-Mudawwanat al-kubra 1:71). 

• Makka (Imam Shafi'i): Based on the practice of the inhabitants of Makka following the teachings of 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr ؓ, favoring raising the hands. 

• Kufa (Imam Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ): Influenced by 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and 'Ali رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ (who moved the caliphate to Kufa) alongside approximately 1,500 Companions. As Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazi noted (quoted by 'Allama 'Iraqi in Sharh al-Taqrib): "We are not aware of any city, in which all its inhabitants had completely abandoned the practice of raising the hands at all instances of ascending or descending in prayer, besides the people of Kufa" (Ithaf al-sadat al-muttaqin 3:54).

f: What remarks did Imam Tirmidhi make regarding the chapters on raising vs. not raising the hands in his Sunan?
b:
• At the end of the chapter on raising hands, he remarked: "This is the opinion of a few [ba'd] Companions".

• At the end of the chapter on not raising hands, he remarked: "This is the opinion of more than one [ghayru wahidin]" (indicating a greater number than ba'd).

These remarks indicate that the practice of not raising the hands was very widespread.

f: What are the three types of hadiths regarding raf' al-yadayn categorized in the text?
b:
1. Those clearly mentioning that the Messenger ﷺ raised his hands at the time of ruku'.

2. Those mentioning that the Messenger ﷺ never raised his hands except when uttering the opening takbir.

3. Those describing the complete prayer of the Messenger ﷺ but not mentioning whether or not he raised his hands after the opening takbir.

f: How do Hanafi scholars use the third category of hadiths (those not mentioning hand raising) alongside the second category?
b:
• Not mentioning something only evidences that it was not a popular practice.

• If raising hands had been an important, regular aspect of prayer, a narrator describing the complete prayer could not have failed to mention it.

• Furthermore, not raising hands is a "nonexistent" action, and people do not mention nonexistent actions in conversation (comparable to someone arriving home without an accident, where nobody remarks "He did not fall").

• Thus, when combined with the second category, hadiths supporting not raising hands actually outnumber those in support of it.

f: What are the seven instances within salat where hadiths report the Messenger ﷺ raising his hands at one time or another?
b: (1) At the initial takbir; (2) before and after bowing (ruku'); (3) before descending into prostration (sajda); (4) between the two prostrations (sujud); (5) when beginning the second rak'a; (6) when beginning the third rak'a; (7) at the change of every new posture in prayer.

f: Why do proponents of raising hands (group one) adopt only the first two instances (opening takbir and ruku') and abandon the rest?
b: Whatever reason group one has for adopting only two instances and abandoning the rest serves as the same reason for Imam Abu Hanifa رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ and Imam Malik to adopt the first instance only and abandon the others.

f: What are the primary sources of evidence for group one versus the Hanafi school regarding raf' al-yadayn?
b:
• Group One: Primarily rely on narrations of Ibn 'Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا and Malik ibn al-Huwayrith ؓ (who reported raising hands at all seven instances, though group one accepted only opening takbir and ruku').

• Hanafi School: Rely on reports whose narrators are consistent, primarily the narrations of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud ؓ, who states that hands were raised at the initial takbir only and not repeated at any other time in the prayer.

f: How did Imam Malik view the narrations of Ibn 'Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا regarding raising hands, given his famous "golden chain" (silsilat al-dhahab)?
b: Although Imam Malik received many narrations from Ibn 'Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا via Nafi' (his famous "golden chain"), he did not base his opinion on them for this issue; instead, he adopted the narrations of Ibn Mas'ud رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ and gave preference to the continuous practice (ta'amul) of the people of Madina, which was to raise hands at the initial takbir only.

f: What inconsistencies are noted in some narrations of Ibn 'Umar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا regarding raising hands?
b: In one narration mentioned in Imam Tahawi's رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ Mushkil al-athar, it states that the hands were raised at every movement of the prayer, whereas in his other narrations, this is not mentioned. This confusion prevents his inconsistent reports from being adopted over more precise and consistent ones.

f: What are the details of the first narration of 'Alqama reporting from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud ؓ concerning raf' al-yadayn?
b:
• 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud ؓ said: "Should I not demonstrate the prayer of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for you?" He performed the prayer, and did not raise his hands except at the initial takbir (Sunan al-Tirmidhi 1:59, Sunan al-Nasa'i 1:161, Sunan Abi Dawud 1:116). 

• Imam Tirmidhi classifies this hadith as sound (hasan), 'Allama ibn Hazm classifies it as rigorously authenticated (sahih) (al-Muhalla 4:88), and 'Allama Ahmad Muhammad Shakir defended its authenticity against criticism.

f: What do 'Alqama's second and third reports from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud ؓ state regarding the Prophet's ﷺ hand-raising?
b:
• Second Report: The Messenger ﷺ stood up and raised his hands at the outset and did not do so again (Sunan al-Nasa'i 1:158, I'la' al-sunan 3:48).
